Please read /papers/investigations-4/12_height_dependent_heat_contours/brainstorm/notes/11_CONTINUATION_FLEXIBLE_ANALYTIC_RH_TO_SIMPLICITY_20261023.md. 

Please begin on the research in the research overview.
I’ll read the continuation note and the repository’s research guidance, then start the first tractable part of the overview and save the findings in the investigation.

The overview leaves the method open, and its main gap is clear: none of the existing formulas yet gives a useful growing-height arithmetic bound on multiplicities. I’m comparing the heat-flow approaches with an arithmetic mean-value route, with separate agents checking the positive-time statistic and relevant literature.

Two concrete improvements are taking shape. A comparison with Hermite-polynomial roots appears to preserve the full multiplicity cost at positive heat time. Separately, a Gaussian calculation for the complete xi function appears to extend the book’s arithmetic anchor from an exponentially small heat interval to one of order \(1/\log T\). I’m checking both proofs and what they actually imply for simplicity.

Both proof checks passed within their stated scope. The literature check also found the Gaussian mechanism in Dobner’s work, so I’m treating the anchor result as a uniform specialization that improves the book’s current bound, without claiming a new representation. The mean-value route I checked gives only the older two-thirds simplicity bound; optimizing that particular input will not improve the current benchmark.
In general, when you find a relevant research article, please place it in a new folder devoted to keeping track of references
I just realized we should've been doing this the whole time

I’ll add a dedicated references folder for this investigation and backfill the papers used in this round and the continuation note, with citations, stable links, and notes on how each is used. I’ll keep downloaded article PDFs outside Git, as the repository’s large-file policy requires.
Please add guidance in the root of the repository

I’ll put the standing guidance in a root-level `REFERENCE_WORKFLOW.md` and link it from the repository README. It will require a reference record when an article is found, including the version, why it matters, and which claims were actually checked.

The research notes and root guidance are saved. The reference collection now contains eight version-pinned articles and two DLMF entries; all eight PDFs are stored outside Git and their hashes have been verified. I’m finishing the link checks and chat-history capture.

Added [root reference guidance](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/REFERENCE_WORKFLOW.md), linked from the README and large-file policy.

Created a [reference collection](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-4/12_height_dependent_heat_contours/references/README.md) with eight versioned articles, BibTeX, usage notes, and verified PDF copies stored outside Git.

The research produced two internally reviewed results:

- [Note 12](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-4/12_height_dependent_heat_contours/brainstorm/notes/12_HERMITE_CLUSTER_DOMINATION_AND_JOINT_CONSUMER_20261023.md): finite-time Hermite domination and the joint bound \(M\le5R/8+3q/2\).
- [Note 13](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-4/12_height_dependent_heat_contours/brainstorm/notes/13_COMPLETE_XI_LOGARITHMIC_HEAT_ANCHOR_20261023.md): an exterior arithmetic anchor valid on heat widths of order \(1/\log T\).

These strengthen supporting estimates; they do **not yet establish a new simplicity proportion**.
What is the strongest path forward?
I’ll compare the new results with the remaining arithmetic gaps and assess which next argument has the best chance of producing a substantive simplicity result.

The comparison points toward a more direct arithmetic approach. Mollified values of \(\zeta'\) at the zeros already lead to a proved simplicity proportion, whereas the heat quantities still lack useful upper bounds. Simply adding a smooth heat weight would stay within the already optimized mollifier class; the next candidate needs a genuinely new arithmetic correlation.

There is a concrete test: find an additional arithmetic weight that improves the mean-square estimate in the existing \(19/27\) argument. That would give a measurable simplicity gain. Prime-factor weights are already known in related mollifier work, so I’m recording that prior art and treating their use at the zeros as a candidate to check—not as a new method yet.

**My judgment: prioritize arithmetic estimates for mollified values of \(\zeta'\) at the zeros.** This currently offers the clearest route to a substantive simplicity result.

The advantage is direct: \(\zeta'(\rho)=0\) at every multiple zero. First and second moments of \(B(\rho)\zeta'(\rho)\) therefore measure simplicity immediately. This is the mechanism behind the RH-conditional \(19/27\) result of [Bui–Heath-Brown](https://arxiv.org/abs/1302.5018v1).

Our heat results provide useful supporting tools, but they still lack the arithmetic upper estimate that restricts actual multiplicities. Further approximation work should serve a specific missing estimate.

I recommend this next calculation:

1. **Use the optimized \(19/27\) argument as the baseline.** Its existing smooth weight is already optimized; changing that weight alone cannot improve it.
2. **Test one richer arithmetic weight**, incorporating prime-factor information. Such weights have prior art in [related mollifier work](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40687-019-0199-8); their usefulness for our discrete moments needs checking.
3. **Calculate its correlation with the baseline’s remaining error**, together with a rigorous second-moment bound. A nonzero correlation can reduce that error and yield a stronger simplicity bound. All remainder estimates must support the gain.

That gives us a focused research question with a meaningful success or failure outcome. It also identifies exactly where new arithmetic information must enter.

**For every-zero simplicity, a further argument remains necessary:** even a substantially improved average bound can permit sparse double zeros. I cannot yet defend a complete proof strategy for excluding all of them.

I saved the detailed comparison and calculation in [Review 04, Section 5](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-4/12_height_dependent_heat_contours/brainstorm/reviews/04_ANALYTIC_SIMPLICITY_OPENING_ROUND_REVIEW_20261023.md#5-strategic-reassessment-a-direct-arithmetic-comparison), and added the two relevant papers to the reference collection.
Please continue with the research as proposed

I’ll work through the proposed extra arithmetic weight, starting with the published moment formulas and their error estimates. The first objective is to determine whether it improves the simplicity bound or runs into a specific obstruction.

The new weight passes an initial check: it retains the squarefree support and coefficient bounds used in the large-modulus error argument. I also found that an older general moment theorem has an extra coefficient condition this weight fails, so it cannot be applied directly. I’m checking the newer theorem and the remaining main terms.

The first moment is now worked out: for the simplest proposed weight, its normalized limit is \(\theta^2/240\). I also found a way to apply the published moment theorems legally: add a small multiple of the new weight to the existing mollifier, then recover the desired moments by finite differences. The mixed second moment is the next decisive calculation.

The mixed-moment calculation now has a complete published formula to work from. I’m retaining all its main-term contributions; a gain from only the simplest contribution would not establish an improvement. There is also a smoothing issue to resolve before the symbolic calculation can support a theorem.

The complete mixed calculation gives a cancellation: the proposed prime-pair weight has zero correlation with the optimized baseline’s residual. That points to no improvement from this direction. I’m checking the analytic remainder estimates so I can state precisely which class of weights this rules out.

The independent calculation confirms the cancellation. I’m saving the result with its precise scope: sufficiently smoothed two-prime weights give no leading-order improvement through fixed, nondegenerate combinations. Low-smoothing weights and combinations whose leading moments vanish remain open.

This gives us a useful decision point: further coefficient searches within the tested class are unlikely to help. The next question is whether the same cancellation holds for a broader class, or whether a different arithmetic direction escapes it. I’m recording that distinction and adding the five relevant papers to the reference collection.

The note and internal review are saved. All 50 exact symbolic checks passed, including the complete mixed kernel and residue cancellation. I’m finishing the link and archive checks; the result remains a scoped exclusion of this candidate family, with no improved simplicity proportion.

The proposed two-prime Feng test produced an **exact cancellation**. For sufficiently smoothed profiles, fixed combinations with positive limiting second moment cannot improve the baseline at leading order. This narrows the search; it does not improve the \(19/27\) simplicity bound.

Saved the derivation in [Note 14](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-4/12_height_dependent_heat_contours/brainstorm/notes/14_DISCRETE_FENG_MOMENT_REDUCTION_20261023.md), with an internal review and 50 passing exact symbolic checks. Five additional papers were archived and cataloged.

The strongest next step is to test a structurally different arithmetic direction for **nonzero residual correlation** before undertaking further optimization. Low-smoothing profiles and combinations whose leading moments vanish remain outside the proved exclusion.
Please continue with the research as proposed

I’ll use the cancellation result to test a different arithmetic direction, starting with its first and mixed moments. I’ll also check whether the cancellation reflects a broader restriction on one-piece mollifiers.

Two distinct tests are underway: conjugating the derivative-weighted mollifier through the functional equation, and changing the coefficients to include prime powers. I’m also checking how far the previous cancellation extends, so another coefficient change does not merely reproduce it.

The cancellation extends to every fixed order of the smoothed distinct-prime family. The prime-power test also gives no leading gain after correcting for its larger second moment. Conjugation remains outside these exclusions, but its evaluation needs a holomorphic second moment that the existing theorems do not supply; the literature treats even the unmollified analogue as conjectural.

The prime-power test revealed an important normalization issue: its second moment grows like \(\log T\). After scaling it to a finite limiting norm, both its mean and its correlation with the baseline vanish. That rules out this particular two-dimensional enlargement even with height-dependent mixing coefficients. I’m consolidating the proofs and recording the remaining conjugate-moment problem.
Just checking, are you considering a flow equation for the contour itself, defined by \epsilon(T)?

Not in this last calculation—I’ve been testing arithmetic mollifiers. The earlier contour work allows moving boundaries, but I haven’t yet investigated an evolution equation that determines \(\epsilon(T)\) itself.

That is a distinct direction. I’ll check whether the transport identity can yield such an equation while retaining the full source and error terms, and whether it would control the contour’s admissible width rather than merely prescribe it.
well \epsilon is a function of height and t
It would be interesting to investigate what kind of evolution equations might be natural for the contour

I’ll investigate evolution laws for \(\epsilon(T,t)\), treating height \(T\) and heat time \(t\) as independent variables. I’ll compare contours transported by the zero motion with contours defined by an analytic level set, and check what each law would need to control.

I’m carrying forward the original backward-time contour as a moving face �τ=t−ε(T,t). Is that the geometry you mean, or are you instead thinking of a spatial contour Im z=ε(T,t) at heat time t?
- Moving backward-time face τ=t−ε(T,t)
- Spatial contour Im z=ε(T,t)

The existing notes already contain a useful starting point: a contour that follows levels of the first-jet ratio \(H/H_z\). That motion cancels one boundary flux exactly. The question is whether it also gives a controllable evolution for \(\epsilon(T,t)\), especially where the contour bends or its level-set description breaks down.

For the original backward-time face \(s=t-\epsilon(T,t)\), a natural candidate is
\[
\epsilon_t+v(s,T)\epsilon_T=0,
\]
where \(v\) transports the first-jet coordinate \(H/H_z\). This gives an evolution law for the contour, but it only transports the chosen width. I’m also examining a law that adjusts the width using a provable boundary margin, which is where a useful estimate could enter.

Is that the geometry you mean, or are you instead thinking of a spatial contour Im z=ε(T,t) at heat time t?","answer":"The spatial contour as a function of time (if you took t=0 it would just give the \\xi function or the multiple of it as defined by H). I'm thinking of it as kind of a stochastic boundary being buffeted around by zero flux, but on average keeping a relatively well maintained shape."}]
</send_user_message_question_reply>

Understood—you mean the spatial boundary
\[
z=T+i\epsilon(T,t),
\]
moving with the heat flow. I had carried forward the earlier backward-time geometry.

Your picture suggests a useful combination: motion driven by local zero flux, plus a smoothing or restoring term that maintains the contour’s overall shape. I’ll derive that balance first, then examine whether a stochastic description of the fluctuations is justified by averaging the deterministic zero flow.
I'm not even sure if you need the smoothing term. The stochastic zero flux might average out over time.

We may not need it. I’ll first study the boundary driven by zero flux alone.

The distinction to check is whether the accumulated flux stays small. Fluctuations can have zero average velocity yet still make a boundary wander over time. The exact conservation law may give stronger control than that heuristic, so I’ll examine it before adding smoothing.
Yes definitely, these are the types of considerations that depend on the details

There is now a concrete model with no smoothing term. Using the regularized zero density \(\mu\) and current \(j\), the velocity
\[
u=\frac{j}{\lambda+\mu}
\]
transports the contour and exactly conserves “zero mass plus \(\lambda\) times enclosed area,” with any end flux included.

That gives a mechanism for controlling average width. Local roughness and repeated inward crossings require separate estimates. Those are the details I’m recording as the next questions, along with the normalization needed to make the model meaningful at large height.
Does this preserve the integral along the line? I'm starting to think that can control the motion, preserving the value of the integral
Or some kind of Lagrangian

The current model preserves enclosed augmented mass, not automatically a line integral. Your Lagrangian suggestion gives another natural law.

For example, if the integral is \(\int_{\Gamma_t}H(t,z)\,dz\), then choosing the contour-point velocity
\[
\dot z=\frac{H_z}{H}
\]
preserves that integral on every material segment, wherever \(H\ne0\). This follows from \(H_t=-H_{zz}\). I’ll check this against the integral you want to preserve and distinguish preservation of the whole integral from preservation along each segment.

Which line integral do you have in mind for the spatial contour? I’m deriving the general preservation law while checking these possibilities.
- The integral of H(t,z) dz
- The zero-counting integral (H_z/H) dz
- The earlier phase or topological integral

I’m deriving the general preservation law while checking these possibilities.","answer":"I had the topological integral in mind but I think it is worth looking into all possibilities and see which is most natural"}]

I’ll compare all three. For the topological integral, there is an important distinction: its total value is already unchanged by deformations that avoid singularities, so preserving that total may not determine the contour’s motion.

A more restrictive Lagrangian condition is to preserve the relevant differential form on each material piece. That leads to different candidate velocities for \(H\,dz\), the zero-counting form, and the physical first jet \((H,H_z)\). I’m checking which best matches the original topological construction.

There is a useful connection: the same unsmoothed current law has a genuine first-order Lagrangian, and it preserves a specific circulation integral around a closed material contour.

I’m now checking the version built from the physical jet \((H,H_z)\). Its connection form is the one underlying the original Chern–Hopf integral, so it may be the most natural way to turn your topological idea into a contour equation. Preserving that circulation and preserving the full topological charge are distinct conditions.
I'm thinking of the flux as a source to a conservation law. Finding the conservation law is key. You already mentioned the integral of H as a conservation law. That may be the most natural.
Finding the most natural conservation law is key

The heat equation itself now gives the strongest candidate:
\[
H_t+\partial_z(H_z)=0.
\]
It selects the Lagrangian velocity \(u=H_z/H\), which preserves \(H\,dz\) on each material segment.

There is also a positive-density version:
\[
\partial_t|H|^2+\nabla\!\cdot(H_z\overline H)=0,
\]
with the complex current read as a planar vector. It gives the same velocity. I’ll make this the primary candidate and compare it with the topological flow. The main limitation to investigate is that \(u\) is singular at zeros of \(H\).
Yes, I'm getting my intuition from Noether's theorem
These are powerful tools used in integrable systems

Yes—the logarithmic derivative puts this directly into the Burgers/Cole–Hopf framework. With \(p=H_z/H\),
\[
p_t+\partial_z(p_z+p^2)=0.
\]
The heat equation’s adjoint formulation also gives a family of conservation laws, with the \(H\,dz\) law as the simplest case.

That gives us a principled comparison: which conserved density produces a contour flow that stays regular and makes the original integral easier to estimate? I’ll work from those identities rather than prescribe a boundary shape.
Make sure to include these references in the citation list
I’ll add the Cole–Hopf and Noether/adjoint references to the investigation’s citation list, record which passages were checked, and archive accessible PDFs under the repository’s reference policy.
Sometimes you can get an infinite hierarchy of conserved quantities

Yes—and here we can write one explicitly. If
\[
\psi_n(t,z)=e^{t\partial_z^2}z^n,
\]
then
\[
\partial_t(\psi_nH)+\partial_z(\psi_nH_z-\psi_{n,z}H)=0.
\]
The first weights are \(1,\ z,\ z^2+2t,\ z^3+6tz,\ldots\).

These give conserved integrals when the endpoint fluxes vanish, or when the corresponding material endpoints are used. The next question is whether one member—or a useful combination—controls the contour’s behavior near zeros.
I think it probably has to

It may. I’ll test the hierarchy jointly using the actual theta values of the invariants. The concrete question is whether they bound contour deformation as \(H\) becomes small; a single conserved weighted integral can allow large motion there.

The primitive formulation gives a precise starting point: \(P_z=H\), \(P_t=-H_z\), and \(P(t,Z(t))\) is constant along the proposed motion. It also has a Noether action whose conserved quantities are \(\Re P\) and \(\Im P\).
An infinite hierarchy is pretty rigid usually

Yes. Here the complete Fourier hierarchy actually determines the evolving field:
\[
e^{-t\xi^2}\widehat H_t(\xi)=\widehat H_0(\xi).
\]
So the rigidity is real. The question is how to turn it into a useful bound on contour deformation or the first jet, using the specific theta initial data. That is a stronger direction than assuming that the flux simply averages to zero.

The useful distinction is between having an infinite hierarchy and having the specific conserved values supplied by the theta kernel. I’m checking that distinction against collision examples, so we can identify what additional estimate would turn the hierarchy’s rigidity into control of the contour.

The check confirms that even a complete conserved hierarchy can coexist with a zero collision: an explicit Gaussian heat solution preserves all these quantities while developing a double zero. The promising step is therefore to use the **theta-specific values** to bound contour strain or proximity to critical values. I’m saving that distinction alongside the Noether derivations and references.

The derivations and review are saved. The primary model is \(u=H_z/H\), which preserves \(H\,dz\) on material subarcs. The notes distinguish the hierarchy’s uniqueness statement from the quantitative contour control still needed. I also updated the citation list and checked the archived references.

Yes—and here we can make that precise: **the full Fourier hierarchy determines the entire heat evolution**:
\[
e^{-t\xi^2}\widehat H(t,\xi)=\widehat H(0,\xi).
\]

The distinction is between having the conservation laws and having **their specific theta values**. I checked explicit decaying heat solutions that preserve a complete hierarchy yet develop double zeros. Their conserved values differ from theta’s.

The strongest next step is therefore to extract a quantitative bound from the theta values—controlling deformation of the contour transported by \(u=H_z/H\), which preserves \(H\,dz\). The hierarchy supplies rigidity; we still need the inequality connecting it to geometry and collision-sensitive flux.

I saved the derivations and checks in [Note 16](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-4/12_height_dependent_heat_contours/brainstorm/notes/16_NATURAL_CONTOUR_EVOLUTION_20261023.md), and added the Noether, Cole–Hopf and adjoint-method sources to the [citation list](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-4/12_height_dependent_heat_contours/references/README.md).

Please include this in the manuscript. We want to include this in the book, but I don't think it is ready yet, so include it in main.tex. Please create a new research-overview document and corresponding research-progress file, verify the chat records, and provide a continuation note to continue with the research.
I’ll add the conservation-law research to `main.tex` as provisional material, create a focused overview and progress file, then verify the chat archive and write a continuation note.

The working draft already has separate sections, so I’ll add a conservation-law section there with proofs, references and explicit open questions. I’m using the write-page skill for the handoff documents and the PDF skill to check the compiled manuscript.
When writing the research-overview, please focus on analytical results that are working toward the result and proof that will eventually go in the book

I’ll center the overview on analytic results that could become part of the book’s proof: estimates using the actual theta invariants, control of contour deformation and inward flux, and the resulting simplicity consequence. The formal identities will serve as the starting point; computations will support specific proof questions.
Numerics are always in a supporting role
Understood. I’ll state that explicitly: numerics support a named analytic argument or test a proposed estimate; they are not separate research goals.

The review identified an important continuation issue: avoiding primitive critical values is not enough, because an inverse branch can also escape toward a finite asymptotic value. I’m making branch containment and actual tangent deformation part of the analytic task, alongside the source estimate needed to prove them.

The expanded draft compiles cleanly to 27 pages, and the PDF layout checks passed. The new overview is organized around a concrete analytic estimate and the proof obligations needed to turn it into contour control. It keeps the microscopic estimate proposed during this review explicitly unproved.

All six local chat records passed their integrity checks, and this chat matches the completed public transcript. The wider scan also confirmed unique registrations. It found an unrelated archive index with existing merge-conflict markers; I left it untouched and recorded that caveat in the verification receipt.

The manuscript and handoff documents now make that explicit: analytical results and proofs drive the program; numerics support specific estimates. The continuation note identifies the next unproved estimate and the steps needed to turn it into contour control.

Added the conservation laws, Noether formulation, and hierarchy discussion to [main.tex](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-4/12_height_dependent_heat_contours/manuscript/main.tex). It remains provisional; `book.tex` is unchanged.
